lessons.title: Day 1 — Constitutional basics, aptitude and economics
lessons.intro: A two-hour foundation session in Constitution, aptitude and economics. The 15 questions are original practice, not reproduced APPSC past-paper questions. Keep the full-paper diagnostic for a separate two-hour session.

schedule.title: Constitution: read, make a memory table, recall without looking
Economics: scarcity, opportunity cost and demand

sections.title: Constitution
paragraphs: Adoption: 26 November 1949. General commencement: 26 January 1950; some provisions began earlier. Do not interchange these dates.

The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 introduced Socialist, Secular and integrity into the Preamble. These changes took effect on 3 January 1977. The Preamble identifies constitutional ideals; it is not a list of individually enforceable claims.

Part III contains Fundamental Rights; Part IV contains Directive Principles; Part IVA contains Fundamental Duties. Article 37 makes Directive Principles non-enforceable by courts, while treating them as fundamental to governance.

Article 14: equality protection for persons. Article 19: specified freedoms for citizens. Article 21: life/personal-liberty protection for persons. Article 32: Supreme Court remedy for enforcing Fundamental Rights. Article 51A: Fundamental Duties of citizens.

Activity: spend 10 minutes reading, 10 making an article→meaning→beneficiary table, 10 reconstructing it with the notes covered, and 5 correcting errors. Trap: a non-citizen is not excluded from every Fundamental Right.

sections.title: Aptitude
paragraphs: Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. Always identify the base. A 10% rise followed by a 10% fall takes 100 → 110 → 99: a 1% net fall, not zero.
For a ratio a:b, the first share of total T is aT/(a+b). Example: divide 50 in the ratio 2:3: the shares are 20 and 30.
Mean = total ÷ count, so total = mean × count. If five values average 12, their total is 60. If four of them average 11, the remaining value is 60 − 44 = 16.
Activity: spend 5 minutes understanding the three methods, 5 redoing the examples without looking, and 5 explaining why adding successive percentage rates can fail.

sections.title: Official-notice reading
paragraphs: Read APPSC's addendum dated 13 October 2026. It applies to notifications 07/2026, 08/2026 and 19/2026; Group I 07/2026 is one of the notifications covered here.

Its note allows candidates in the listed SC/ST/BC/EWS/PBD categories who use upper-age relaxation to be considered for open-competition vacancies. Consideration is not guaranteed selection. The notice does not tell you to change your community category to OC.

Activity: record the issuing body, date, affected notification numbers and one precise effect. Then state one conclusion the notice does not support. This is official-source reading practice; it is not a full current-affairs digest.

sections.title: Economics foundation
paragraphs: Scarcity means limited resources have competing uses, so choices are necessary. Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative forgone, not the sum of every rejected alternative. If your best alternative to studying pays ₹300, choosing study forgoes ₹300.

A change in a good's own price, holding other relevant factors constant, causes movement along its demand curve. A fall in price normally increases quantity demanded. Changes in income, tastes or related-goods prices can shift the curve.
For a normal good, higher income shifts demand rightward: more is demanded at each unchanged price. Keep increase in quantity demanded (movement) separate from increase in demand (shift).

Absolute price elasticity = |percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price|. Above 1: elastic; below 1: inelastic; equal to 1: unit elastic. When told to use initial values, divide quantity change by initial quantity and price change by initial price; do not silently switch to midpoint percentages.
Worked example: price ₹20 → ₹22 is +10%; quantity 100 → 80 is −20%. Using initial-value percentages, absolute elasticity = 20/10 = 2.

Activity: read for 10 minutes, draw one movement and one shift for 5, redo the numerical example for 5, then spend 10 explaining scarcity, opportunity cost and the movement/shift distinction without notes. This begins the foundation; the eventual AD papers demand postgraduate-standard preparation.

questions.prompt: On which date was the Constitution adopted?
questions.explanation: Adoption was on 26 November 1949; general commencement was on 26 January 1950.

questions.prompt: Which set of words was introduced into the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976?
questions.explanation: The amendment introduced Socialist and Secular, and added integrity to the existing unity wording.

questions.prompt: Which provision expressly grants its listed freedoms to citizens?
options: All three equally restrict protection to citizens
questions.explanation: Article 19 addresses citizens. Articles 14 and 21 use person, a broader category.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Directive Principles is correct?
options: Each is directly enforceable under Article 32
They are non-enforceable by courts but fundamental to governance
questions.explanation: Article 37 distinguishes lack of direct court enforcement from their importance in governance.

questions.prompt: Where are Fundamental Duties located?
questions.explanation: Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA under Article 51A.

questions.prompt: Article 32 principally guarantees a remedy in the Supreme Court for what purpose?
questions.explanation: Article 32 concerns enforcement of Fundamental Rights, not every legal dispute.

questions.prompt: A price rises by 20% and then falls by 20%. Relative to the original price, it is now:
questions.explanation: Take 100: 100 × 1.20 × 0.80 = 96. The second percentage uses the increased base.

questions.prompt: 64 is divided in the ratio 3:5. What is the smaller share?
questions.explanation: There are 8 ratio parts. Each is 64/8 = 8; the smaller share is 3 × 8 = 24.

questions.prompt: Four numbers average 18. The first three average 16. What is the fourth number?
questions.explanation: All four total 4 × 18 = 72. The first three total 3 × 16 = 48. Difference: 24.

questions.prompt: A town can fund repairs to its library or its bus shelter this month, but not both. This illustrates:
options: Making a choice removes all future needs
questions.explanation: Scarcity means resources are insufficient for all competing uses, so choices must be made.

questions.prompt: Meena studies for two hours. Her next-best alternative was a typing assignment paying ₹400. Studying has no additional expense. What is the opportunity cost?
questions.explanation: The value of the next-best alternative forgone is the ₹400 payment, despite no cash expenditure on studying.

questions.prompt: Rice becomes cheaper and purchases increase, with income, tastes and all other relevant factors unchanged. This is:
options: A downward movement along the existing demand curve
An upward movement along the existing curve
questions.explanation: A change in the good's own price produces movement along the demand curve; no other demand determinant changed.

questions.prompt: Milk is a normal good for a household. Income rises while its price and other relevant factors remain unchanged. Demand:
options: Moves upward along the same curve
Moves downward along the same curve
questions.explanation: Higher income raises demand for a normal good at each price, shifting the curve rightward.

questions.prompt: Price rises from ₹40 to ₹44 and quantity demanded falls from 100 to 85. Using INITIAL values as the percentage bases, what is absolute price elasticity?
questions.explanation: Price rises 4/40 = 10%; quantity falls 15/100 = 15%. Absolute elasticity = 15/10 = 1.5, elastic. This is the specified initial-value method, not midpoint elasticity.

questions.prompt: Under the 13 October 2026 APPSC addendum, a candidate from a listed category who uses upper-age relaxation:
options: Must change community category to OC
Is automatically appointed to an OC vacancy
Can also be considered for OC vacancies
Is excluded from every OC vacancy
questions.explanation: The note permits consideration for open-competition vacancies. It neither guarantees appointment nor directs a change of community category.

lessons.intro: Continue Day 1 with rights and remedies, percentage applications and the Tuesday Executive Officer specialist slot. The first 60 minutes build common skills for all five notification tracks; the next 30 minutes introduce EO Paper II. Finish with 15 original practice questions and error review. These notes and questions are independently prepared learning material, not an official APPSC paper or a prediction of questions. The EO block is an introduction, not completion of its specialist syllabus. Use the time limits for reading, worked examples and recall together.

sections.title: Fundamental Rights: identify the right, its beneficiary and its remedy
paragraphs: Time plan: spend 3 minutes recalling Day 1's Parts III, IV and IVA; 17 minutes on the article map below; 8 minutes comparing the two writ jurisdictions; and 7 minutes writing a closed-book recall table. Classification matters more than memorising isolated article numbers.

Article 14: the State must respect equality before law and equal protection of the laws for any person within India. Its wording is not limited to citizens. Do not turn equality into the claim that every distinction is forbidden: constitutionally permitted special provisions and reservations have to be read with their own clauses.

Articles 15 and 16: Article 15(1) prohibits State discrimination against citizens only on religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. Article 16 concerns equality of opportunity for citizens in employment or appointment under the State. Keep the contexts separate: a question about public employment points to Article 16. Article 16(2) also names descent and residence; do not mechanically copy the Article 15 list. These articles contain further clauses allowing specified special provisions; the basic prohibitions are not a complete reservation rulebook.

Article 19: six freedoms are stated for citizens—speech and expression; peaceful assembly without arms; associations, unions or co-operative societies; movement throughout India; residence and settlement; and profession, occupation, trade or business. They are subject to the restrictions specified in the article. The right to property is not one of these six current freedoms. Exam trap: neither 'available only to citizens' nor 'available to every person' is correct for every Fundamental Right.

Article 21 protects every person's life and personal liberty against deprivation except according to procedure established by law. Article 21A requires the State to provide free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14, in the manner determined by law. Compare Article 45 in Part IV: it concerns early childhood care and education below age 6. Keep the age ranges and constitutional categories distinct.

Article 32 guarantees the right to approach the Supreme Court through appropriate proceedings to enforce Part III rights. Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue directions, orders and writs for Part III rights and for other purposes. Thus Article 226 has a wider subject-matter reach for writ relief; this does not mean a High Court is above the Supreme Court. Article 226 is in Part VI, not Part III. Territorial and other legal requirements still apply.

Writ memory cues: habeas corpus examines the legality of detention; mandamus calls for performance of a public legal duty; prohibition restrains proceedings beyond jurisdiction; certiorari can quash an unlawful decision on recognised grounds; quo warranto questions the legal authority to occupy a public office. These are study cues, not exhaustive legal tests. Remember 'detention—habeas corpus' and 'public office—quo warranto' before learning finer distinctions.

Rights, principles and duties: Part III supplies Fundamental Rights and constitutional remedies. Article 37 says Part IV principles are not enforceable by a court, while treating them as fundamental to governance and making their application in lawmaking a duty of the State. Part IVA, Article 51A, lists citizens' Fundamental Duties. A desirable welfare objective does not become an Article 32 claim merely because it appears in Part IV; check whether a separate enforceable right or law is involved.

Worked classification: a question asks about a ten-year-old child's constitutional entitlement to free compulsory education. Choose Article 21A, not Article 45 or the general freedom provisions of Article 19. A separate question asks which article specifically protects equality of opportunity in State employment: choose Article 16, even though Article 14 supplies the broader equality principle.

Closed-book task: draw three columns—article, beneficiary/context, key protection. Fill 14, 15, 16, 19, 21, 21A, 32 and 226. Then write two differences between Articles 32 and 226 and the three-way distinction between Parts III, IV and IVA. Reopen the notes only after finishing. Mark any confused pair for the final review block.

sections.title: Percentage applications: always name the base
paragraphs: Time plan: 4 minutes on the rules, 7 minutes reproducing the examples on paper, and 4 minutes checking the short recall task. Percent means per hundred, but the denominator decides what the answer means. Write the original value before calculating a percentage change.

Core rules: percentage change = (new value − old value) / old value × 100. An increase of r% multiplies a value by (1 + r/100); a decrease multiplies it by (1 − r/100). Successive changes use successive multiplication, because the second percentage acts on the changed value.

Worked example 1—successive changes: a quantity of 500 rises 20% and then falls 20%. It becomes 500 × 1.20 × 0.80 = 480. The net change is −20/500 × 100 = −4%. Equal percentage increases and decreases do not cancel. With an increase of a% followed by a decrease of a%, the net percentage change is −a²/100.

Worked example 2—reverse percentage: a price after a 15% increase is ₹690. Original price = 690/1.15 = ₹600. Subtracting 15% of ₹690 would use the wrong base. For a known final value, divide by the multiplier that produced it.

Worked example 3—percentage points: a rate rises from 40% to 50%. The rise is 10 percentage points; the relative increase is (50 − 40)/40 × 100 = 25%. In economy or statistics questions, check whether the question asks for a difference between rates or a proportional change in a rate.

Worked example 4—constant spending: if unit price rises 25%, the affordable quantity under an unchanged budget becomes 1/1.25 = 0.80 of its former value. Quantity must fall 20%. Check with a ₹1,000 budget: at ₹40 per unit buy 25 units; at ₹50 buy 20 units. The reduction is 5/25, not 5/20.

Recall task, then check: (a) 200 increased by 10% and then 10% again is 242, a 21% total rise; (b) a value of 360 after a 10% fall came from 400; (c) a rate changing from 8% to 10% rises by 2 percentage points and by 25% relative to its original rate. If any answer differs, circle the denominator you used. All numerical examples in this section are original teaching examples.

The saved current scheme has two objective papers, each with 150 questions, 150 minutes and 150 marks, and one-third negative marking. This reading exercise does not announce a new circular or a new exam date.

Notice the syllabus references to Vedas and Upanishads: these explain today's EO specialist topic. The full Paper II also includes other philosophy, cultural, legal and temple-administration topics. Completing today's introductory notes does not cover the complete paper.

An archived EO paper remains useful for question style and retrieval practice, but its recruitment year, format and syllabus may differ. Start from the current notification and any applicable later official amendment, then label old questions as within the current syllabus, changed, or outside it. When checking an archived paper, prefer that paper's final official key over its initial key. Never transfer an old exam date into the current recruitment.

Ten-minute output: write a six-line scheme card from the official document, then write one sentence explaining why a historical question paper cannot by itself establish the current exam pattern. If a PDF is temporarily unavailable, bookmark the official link and use the saved scheme only as a provisional reading aid; do not infer a new rule from an unavailable page.

sections.title: EO Paper II foundation: textual families and philosophical schools
paragraphs: Time plan: 8 minutes for the four Vedas and textual layers, 7 minutes for selected Upanishad associations, 7 minutes for the six schools, and 8 minutes for closed-book matching. This is the Tuesday EO specialist block in the saved rotation. Other post tracks can use it for cultural awareness, but its specialist relevance is Executive Officer Paper II.

Four Vedas, four recall cues: Rigveda—hymns; Samaveda—chants and their musical rendering; Yajurveda—sacrificial formulae and ritual performance; Atharvaveda—prayers and material concerning varied aspects of life. These are broad memory cues, not claims that each collection contains only one kind of material. Spellings such as Rig Veda and Rigveda refer to the same collection.

Textual layers: Samhitas are collections of mantras; Brahmanas explain ritual; Aranyakas develop forest-text reflection; Upanishads emphasise philosophical inquiry. Do not confuse Brahmana, a category of text, with Brahman, a philosophical term, or with Brahma, a deity. Recognise the term in the wording of the question before selecting an answer.

Upanishad associations for today's first matching set: Aitareya—Rigveda; Isha—Shukla Yajurveda; Kena and Chandogya—Samaveda; Mundaka, Mandukya and Prashna—Atharvaveda. Mundaka and Mandukya are different titles, even though both appear in the Atharvaveda group. These examples are a selected learning set, not a complete catalogue.

The Upanishads are associated with the concluding philosophical portion of Vedic literature and are traditionally included in Shruti. The term Vedanta connects to this end or culmination of the Veda. Do not choose 'a fifth Veda' simply because an option mentions an Upanishad. Study the association and type of text before attempting difficult doctrinal interpretation.

The standard six-school list is Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Purva Mimamsa and Vedanta (Uttara Mimamsa). In the classification used here, their astika status concerns recognition of Vedic authority; reducing the classification to a simple modern 'believes in God/does not believe in God' test can mislead. Distinct schools have different arguments and doctrines.

Traditional teacher-school pairs: Nyaya—Gautama; Vaisheshika—Kanada; Samkhya—Kapila; Yoga—Patanjali; Purva Mimamsa—Jaimini; Vedanta/Uttara Mimamsa—Badarayana. Learn these as conventional textual associations. Do not treat them as a precise chronology of when every idea in a tradition first arose.

Active-recall grid: on blank paper, write four Veda names and one cue for each. Next, match Aitareya, Isha, Kena and Mundaka to their Vedas without looking. Finally, cover the teacher names and retrieve all six school-teacher pairs. Check only after completing each set; put a dot beside uncertain answers even if they turn out correct.

One-minute explanation exercise: tell an imaginary learner how a Veda, an Upanishad and a philosophical school differ as categories. A good answer identifies a scriptural collection, a type of philosophical text within the Vedic tradition, and a system of philosophical thought. Keep classification separate from evaluating anyone's religious belief. Agamas, detailed Vedanta schools, temple administration and applicable laws remain for later EO lessons.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes Articles 14 and 19?
options: Both use citizens alone as their beneficiaries
Article 14 covers any person within India; Article 19 states freedoms for citizens
Article 14 is only a Directive Principle; Article 19 is a Fundamental Duty
Article 19 guarantees unlimited exercise of every listed freedom
questions.explanation: Article 14 uses 'any person', while Article 19 begins with citizens. Article 19 also contains specified restrictions. The trap is extending one article's beneficiary wording to every Fundamental Right. Both articles belong to Part III.

questions.prompt: Which article specifically concerns equality of opportunity in employment or appointment under the State?
questions.explanation: Article 16 specifically addresses public employment and appointment. Article 14 provides a broader equality guarantee; Article 15 addresses prohibited discrimination in its own contexts; Article 21A concerns education for children aged 6–14. The word 'specifically' determines the best answer.

questions.prompt: Article 21A's free and compulsory education provision applies to which age range?
questions.explanation: Article 21A specifies children aged six to fourteen. Article 45, a Directive Principle, concerns early childhood care and education below six. Similar subject matter does not make the age limits or constitutional categories interchangeable.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Articles 32 and 226 is correct?
options: Article 32 is in Part IV and is never enforceable
Only the Supreme Court can issue any writ
Article 226 is confined exclusively to Fundamental Rights
Article 32 concerns enforcement of Part III rights; Article 226 also extends to other purposes
questions.explanation: Article 32 guarantees access to the Supreme Court for enforcing Part III rights. Article 226 gives High Courts writ power for Fundamental Rights and other purposes. Its wider subject-matter scope does not place a High Court above the Supreme Court.

questions.prompt: Which writ is most directly associated with examining whether a person's detention is lawful?
questions.explanation: Habeas corpus addresses the legality of detention. Quo warranto concerns authority to hold a public office, mandamus concerns a public legal duty, and prohibition restrains proceedings beyond jurisdiction. Identify the problem before matching the writ name.

questions.prompt: Which description best reflects Article 37?
options: Every Directive Principle can be enforced directly through Article 32
Directive Principles are merely private moral preferences
Directive Principles are not court-enforceable, but are fundamental to governance and must guide State lawmaking
Directive Principles and Article 51A duties are the same constitutional list
questions.explanation: Article 37 combines non-enforceability in court with constitutional importance in governance and the State's duty to apply the principles in making laws. Non-justiciability does not mean irrelevance. Fundamental Duties are separately listed in Part IVA.

questions.prompt: A value rises by 25% and then falls by 20%. Relative to its original value, it is now:
questions.explanation: Multiply the factors: 1.25 × 0.80 = 1.00. For example, 100 becomes 125 and then 100. Subtracting 20 from 25 is invalid because the two percentages use different bases.

questions.prompt: After a 20% discount, an item costs ₹960. What was its price before the discount?
questions.explanation: The final price is 80% of the original, so original = 960/0.80 = ₹1,200. Adding 20% of ₹960 produces ₹1,152 and uses the wrong base. A forward check gives 1,200 × 0.80 = 960.

questions.prompt: A participation rate rises from 30% to 36%. Which pair gives its rise in percentage points and its relative percentage increase, respectively?
questions.explanation: The rate difference is 36 − 30 = 6 percentage points. Relative increase = 6/30 × 100 = 20%. A percentage-point difference and a percentage change answer different questions.

questions.prompt: If the unit price of a product rises by 20%, by what percentage must quantity purchased fall to keep expenditure unchanged?
questions.explanation: New quantity/original quantity = 1/1.20 = 5/6. The reduction is 1/6, or 16⅔%. For example, a ₹120 budget buys 12 units at ₹10 and 10 units at ₹12; the reduction is 2/12, not 2/10.

questions.topic: Official-source reading — current rules and historical papers
questions.prompt: An old EO paper uses a format that differs from the current notification. What is the soundest preparation approach?
options: Assume the historical format overrides every later notification
Discard every old question without checking its topic
Use a coaching prediction as the deciding authority
Follow the current notification and applicable official amendments, and map old questions to the current syllabus
questions.explanation: The current recruitment's official rules govern its scheme. Historical questions remain useful after checking topic relevance, paper year and key status. Their existence does not prove that a previous format or examination date carries into the current recruitment.

questions.prompt: Which Veda is especially associated with chants and their musical rendering?
questions.explanation: Samaveda is the appropriate association for chant and musical rendering. The recall cues distinguish it from Rigvedic hymns and Yajurvedic sacrificial formulae. These cues describe a prominent characteristic, not an exclusive inventory of every text.

questions.prompt: Which Upanishad–Veda association is correct?
questions.explanation: Kena is associated with Samaveda. In today's selected set, Aitareya belongs to Rigveda and Mundaka to Atharvaveda. Build a matching table rather than relying on which title sounds familiar.

questions.prompt: Which is the conventional school–teacher association?
questions.explanation: Nyaya is conventionally associated with Gautama. The other relevant pairs are Yoga—Patanjali, Vaisheshika—Kanada and Purva Mimamsa—Jaimini. The question tests traditional association, not a precise date of origin.

questions.prompt: In the six-school classification used in today's notes, the astika grouping is principally identified by:
options: Recognition of the authority of the Vedas
Having exactly the same doctrine in all six schools
Being one of the four Vedic Samhitas
questions.explanation: This classification uses recognition of Vedic authority. It does not imply identical doctrines, and a philosophical school is not itself a Vedic Samhita. Avoid replacing this technical classification with a simple modern theist/atheist label.

lessons.title: Day 3 — Parliamentary executive, ratios and welfare safeguards
lessons.intro: Build on Days 1 and 2 by linking constitutional offices to responsibility, using ratios and weighted averages, and introducing welfare safeguards. This numbered lesson follows the Wednesday Welfare Officer slot in the saved rotation; it can be studied whenever you reach Day 3. The first 60 minutes develop common skills across the five notification tracks, followed by a 30-minute ASWO/ATWO specialist block and 30 minutes of practice and review. The 15 questions are original learning exercises, not official past-paper questions or a complete mock examination.

schedule.title: Common core: Union and State executive, advice and responsibility
Aptitude: linked ratios, weighted averages and changing totals
Official reading: map Welfare Paper III and identify its historical final key
Welfare specialist: constitutional safeguards, commissions and two protection Acts
Check answers and explanations, correct errors and plan recall

sections.title: Parliamentary executive: who holds office, who advises and who answers to whom?
paragraphs: Time plan: 3 minutes recalling the rights/remedies distinction from Day 2, 15 minutes reading the Union–State comparisons, 10 minutes making the comparison table, and 7 minutes answering the recall prompts without notes. Today's aim is to connect an office, an article and a responsibility; it is not to memorise every executive power in one sitting.

Union starting points: Article 52 provides for the President of India. Article 53 vests the Union's executive power in the President, to be exercised in accordance with the Constitution. Read this together with Article 74: a Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister aids and advises the President. Constitutional vesting of executive power does not mean that the President personally decides all day-to-day policy independently of the ministerial system.

Advice under Article 74: the President acts in accordance with the Council's advice. The President may ask the Council to reconsider advice, but must act in accordance with the advice tendered after reconsideration. Keep 'request reconsideration' distinct from 'reject the reconsidered advice indefinitely'. For an introductory question, state this constitutional rule before discussing exceptional political situations.

Appointments under Article 75(1): the President appoints the Prime Minister; other Union Ministers are appointed by the President on the Prime Minister's advice. Thus 'appointed by the President' and 'recommended by the Prime Minister' describe different parts of the process for other Ministers. Do not substitute the Speaker or the Chief Justice for the appointing authority.

Collective responsibility under Article 75(3): the Union Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the House of the People, or Lok Sabha. The exact House matters. It is not collectively responsible to the Rajya Sabha in the same constitutional sense. Appointment by the President and collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha are different relationships, not contradictory statements.

Membership under Article 75(5): a Minister who is not a member of either House of Parliament for six consecutive months ceases to be a Minister when that period expires. This does not say that every Minister must belong only to the Lok Sabha. The six-month rule is not a general exemption from other constitutional eligibility or disqualification requirements.

State starting points: Article 153 provides for a Governor for each State and permits the same person to be Governor of two or more States. Article 154 vests the State's executive power in the Governor, in accordance with the Constitution. Article 155 provides for the Governor's appointment by the President. A Governor is not elected by the State Legislative Assembly.

State ministerial system: Article 163 provides for a Council headed by the Chief Minister to aid and advise the Governor, except where the Constitution requires the Governor to exercise discretion. Do not turn this exception into a claim of unrestricted personal discretion over all State policy. Under Article 164(1), the Governor appoints the Chief Minister and appoints other Ministers on the Chief Minister's advice. Article 164(2) makes the State Council collectively responsible to the State Legislative Assembly, not to the Legislative Council where one exists.

Comparison table to write from memory: Union—President, Prime Minister, Articles 74/75, Lok Sabha. State—Governor, Chief Minister, Articles 163/164, Legislative Assembly. Add a second row for formal executive-power provisions: 53 at Union level and 154 at State level. Then add the appointing authority for the Prime Minister, Governor and Chief Minister.

Worked distinction: if a question asks who formally appoints other State Ministers, answer 'the Governor, on the Chief Minister's advice'. If it asks to which House the entire State Council is collectively responsible, answer 'the Legislative Assembly'. A single familiar word such as 'Governor' should not be used to answer both questions.

Closed-book checks: explain why 'executive power vested in the President' must be read with Article 74; complete the sequence 'President may seek reconsideration → Council reconsiders → ...'; and name the correct lower House for collective responsibility at each level. Mark any confusion between appointment, advice and accountability for the final review.

sections.title: Ratios and weighted averages: reconstruct the total before dividing
paragraphs: Time plan: 3 minutes on the rules, 8 minutes reproducing the worked examples, and 4 minutes on the short checks. Day 1 introduced ratios and averages; today use them when groups have different sizes or when the total changes. All numerical examples are original teaching examples.

Ratio rule: if A:B = a:b, write A = ak and B = bk for a common multiplier k. With total T, A = aT/(a+b) and B = bT/(a+b). The ratio numbers are relative parts, not necessarily the actual quantities. If the ratio concerns counts or measurements, keep the units consistent.

Worked example 1—divide a total: 360 books are divided between two libraries in the ratio 4:5. There are 9 equal parts, so each part is 40 books. The libraries receive 160 and 200. Check both their sum, 360, and the simplified ratio, 4:5.

Worked example 2—link two ratios: A:B = 2:3 and B:C = 4:5. Make B equal in both: 2:3 becomes 8:12 and 4:5 becomes 12:15. Therefore A:B:C = 8:12:15. Joining the original numbers as 2:3:5 would incorrectly treat two different B values as equal.

Weighted-average rule: combined mean = total of all observations / total number of observations. If groups have sizes n1 and n2 and means m1 and m2, use (n1m1 + n2m2)/(n1+n2). The mean of the two means works only when their group sizes are equal. A final mean should lie between the group means when all group sizes are positive.

Worked example 3—unequal groups: 20 learners have a mean score of 60 and 30 learners have a mean score of 70. Total score = 20×60 + 30×70 = 3,300; combined mean = 3,300/50 = 66. The answer is closer to 70 because the group with mean 70 is larger. The unweighted answer 65 ignores group sizes.

Worked example 4—remove an observation: ten values have mean 18, so their total is 180. Remove the value 27: new total = 153 and new count = 9; new mean = 17. Update both the numerator and the denominator. If instead a new value x is added, write new total = old total + x and new count = old count + 1.

Quick checks, then verify: (a) 210 divided in the ratio 2:5 gives 60 and 150; (b) two equally sized groups with means 40 and 60 have combined mean 50; (c) five numbers with mean 12 total 60, and adding 18 gives a six-number mean of 13. Before accepting an answer, check the units, the group count and whether the answer is plausible.

Its written scheme lists three degree-standard objective papers, each with 150 questions, 150 minutes and 150 marks: 450 marks in total. Each wrong answer attracts a deduction of one-third of that question's marks. Record this as the current notification's scheme, not as a newly issued update.

In Paper III, map item 2 on government structure and the parliamentary executive to today's common-core block. Map items 7–8 on safeguards, welfare mechanisms, commissions, the atrocities law and legislation against social evils to today's specialist block. Write one line connecting each study block to a syllabus item. This is a method for deciding relevance, not a claim about how many questions the examiner will set from it.

Use 4 minutes to inspect the library entries for the historical Welfare Paper III examination held in 2017 under notification 34/2016. The question-paper file carries an initial key; the official recruitment archive records publication of the separate final key on 22 January 2018. Match the recruitment, paper, Question IDs and option mapping before scoring. A displayed question number or option order may differ in another candidate version. The final key's publication year does not change the paper into a 2018 examination.

Use the final 2 minutes to make an identity card: current notification 26/2026; target Paper III; two relevant syllabus items; historical recruitment 34/2016; examination year 2017; final-key publication 22 January 2018, confirmed in the official archive. A final key governs that historical paper's marking, but does not prove that all its topics, facts or rules are unchanged today. This exercise announces no new circular or examination date.

sections.title: Welfare safeguards: separate the right, the directive, the commission and the statute
paragraphs: Time plan: 8 minutes for Articles 17 and 46, 7 minutes for Articles 338 and 338A, 7 minutes comparing the two Acts, and 8 minutes making a four-column recall chart. This is the Wednesday ASWO/ATWO specialist rotation. The constitutional ideas also support General Studies, but this introductory block does not cover every welfare scheme, reservation provision or protection law in the specialist syllabus.

Article 17, in Part III, abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form. Enforcing a disability arising from untouchability is an offence punishable according to law. This is a Fundamental Right provision, not merely a recommendation to a welfare department. Link it to Day 2's distinction between an enforceable right and a Directive Principle.

Article 46, in Part IV, directs the State to promote the educational and economic interests of weaker sections, especially Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and protect them against social injustice and exploitation. Read it with Article 37: Directive Principles guide governance and lawmaking but are not, by themselves, enforceable by a court. Article 46 does not specify one universal scholarship amount or one reservation percentage for every setting.

Articles 338 and 338A identify two different constitutional commissions: Article 338—National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC); Article 338A—National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST). Both have safeguard-monitoring and complaint-inquiry functions within their constitutional mandates. Their duties include reporting to the President on how safeguards operate and making recommendations. Do not merge them into a single present-day commission or confuse a commission with a ministry administering a scheme.

Institutional distinction: the commissions have specified civil-court powers when investigating or inquiring into the matters described by their articles. This does not make them criminal trial courts or give every recommendation the status of a court judgment. For an exam classification question, first identify whether the body monitors safeguards, administers a programme, investigates an offence or tries a case; these functions are not interchangeable.

Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955: learn its title, year and connection to untouchability. It provides punishment for preaching or practising untouchability and for enforcement of a disability arising from it, along with related matters. It should not be treated as a statute covering every possible civil right merely because its title contains the words 'civil rights'.

Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989: learn its distinct identity and purpose—preventing specified offences of atrocities against members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. Its framework includes Special Courts and Exclusive Special Courts for trial of offences and relief and rehabilitation for victims. It is a separate enactment from the 1955 Act; the two titles are not alternate names for one law. Detailed offences, elements, procedures and amended rules require their own later study.

Worked classification: a question asks for the constitutional abolition of untouchability—Article 17. A question asks for the directive on educational and economic advancement of weaker sections—Article 46. A question asks for the national constitutional commission for Scheduled Tribes—Article 338A. A question asks for the 1989 atrocities-prevention law—name that Act, not the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955.

Recall chart: make columns for instrument, category, purpose and common confusion. Fill five rows: Article 17; Article 46; Article 338; Article 338A; and a comparison row for the 1955/1989 Acts. Cover the names and identify each instrument from its purpose. Then explain why the existence of a constitutional commission does not mean that it replaces the courts or every executive welfare agency.

One-minute retrieval: say aloud '17—Fundamental Right; 46—Directive Principle; 338—NCSC; 338A—NCST; 1955—civil-rights protection connected to untouchability; 1989—prevention of specified atrocities against SC/ST members'. Use this as a memory scaffold, then return to the precise wording when practising more detailed questions.

questions.prompt: Which statement best reads Articles 53 and 74 together?
options: The Prime Minister is the constitutional President of India
Executive power is vested in the President, alongside the constitutional system of ministerial aid and advice
Article 53 removes the need for a Council of Ministers
The Speaker advises the President on every executive decision
questions.explanation: Article 53 vests Union executive power in the President. Article 74 supplies the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister and the advice framework. Reading the provisions together avoids mistaking formal vesting of power for unrestricted independent personal government.

questions.prompt: Under Article 75(5), a Union Minister who is not a member of either House of Parliament for six consecutive months:
options: Automatically becomes a nominated Rajya Sabha member
May continue indefinitely without parliamentary membership
Ceases to be a Minister when that period expires
Must obtain membership only of the Lok Sabha
questions.explanation: The constitutional rule is cessation as Minister at the end of six consecutive months without membership of either House. It does not create automatic nomination or require Lok Sabha membership alone. Other eligibility and disqualification rules still matter.

questions.prompt: The Union Council of Ministers is collectively responsible under Article 75(3) to:
questions.explanation: Article 75(3) specifies the House of the People, which is the Lok Sabha. Do not confuse the President's appointing role with the House to which the Council is collectively responsible.

questions.prompt: After the President asks the Council of Ministers to reconsider advice under Article 74, what does the Constitution provide about the advice tendered after reconsideration?
options: The Speaker must replace the advice with a separate decision
The President may reject it indefinitely without qualification
It automatically becomes a Supreme Court order
The President shall act in accordance with that reconsidered advice
questions.explanation: The proviso to Article 74 permits a request for reconsideration and requires the President to act in accordance with the advice tendered after it. The power to seek reconsideration is not an unlimited power to disregard the resulting advice.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a State Governor is correct?
options: The Governor is elected by the Legislative Assembly
The President appoints the Governor, and one person may be Governor of two or more States
The Chief Minister appoints the Governor for a single State only
The Chief Justice appoints the Governor after each Assembly election
questions.explanation: Article 155 provides for appointment by the President. Article 153 permits the same person to be Governor of two or more States. Neither popular election nor appointment by the Chief Minister is the rule stated in these provisions.

questions.prompt: In a State with both a Legislative Assembly and a Legislative Council, the State Council of Ministers is collectively responsible under Article 164(2) to:
options: Both Houses jointly, in identical terms
questions.explanation: Article 164(2) names the Legislative Assembly. The presence of an upper House does not change the specified House for collective responsibility. Compare this with the Union Council's responsibility to the Lok Sabha.

questions.topic: Aptitude — dividing a total in a ratio
questions.prompt: A total of 640 books is divided between two libraries in the ratio 3:5. How many books does the larger share contain?
questions.explanation: There are 3+5=8 equal parts. Each part is 640/8=80 books, so the larger share is 5×80=400. The remaining 240 gives the required ratio 240:400=3:5.

questions.prompt: If A:B = 3:4 and B:C = 2:5, what is A:B:C?
questions.explanation: Make B equal in the two ratios. Multiply B:C=2:5 by 2 to obtain 4:10, then combine with A:B=3:4. The resulting ratio is 3:4:10. Check that 4:10 simplifies to 2:5.

questions.prompt: Thirty candidates have a mean score of 52 and twenty other candidates have a mean score of 67 on the same test. What is their combined mean?
questions.explanation: Combined score = 30×52 + 20×67 = 1,560+1,340 = 2,900. Divide by 50 candidates to get 58. The simple average 59.5 ignores the unequal group sizes. The combined mean is closer to 52, the mean of the larger group.

questions.topic: Aptitude — adding a value to an average
questions.prompt: Eight values have mean 15. A ninth value is added and the mean becomes 17. What is the ninth value?
questions.explanation: The original total is 8×15=120. The new total is 9×17=153. The added value is 153−120=33. Subtracting the means alone would ignore the change in the number of observations.

questions.topic: Official reading — paper and key identity
questions.prompt: A Welfare Paper III was examined in 2017 under notification 34/2016, and the official archive records its final-key publication on 22 January 2018. Which record is correct?
options: It is a 2018 examination because the final key appeared in 2018
It belongs to notification 26/2026 because it remains useful today
It is a 2017 paper with a 2018 final-key publication; match Question IDs and option mapping before scoring
The initial key should always override the separate final key
questions.explanation: Recruitment number, examination date and verified key-publication date are separate identifiers. Match the historical paper, Question IDs and relevant option mapping before applying the final key. A paper's usefulness does not move it into the current recruitment or make its old rules automatically current.

questions.prompt: Which constitutional provision abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form?
questions.explanation: Article 17 is in Part III and provides the constitutional abolition of untouchability. Article 46 is a Directive Principle on educational and economic interests and protection from injustice; Article 338 concerns the NCSC; Article 164 concerns State Ministers.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Article 46 is correct?
options: It fixes a single scholarship amount for every beneficiary
It is the constitutional article establishing the NCST
It is a Directive Principle promoting weaker sections' educational and economic interests, especially those of SCs and STs
It is the article that elects the Governor
questions.explanation: Article 46 is in Part IV and includes educational and economic advancement and protection against social injustice and exploitation. Its emphasis includes Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. It does not itself prescribe a universal scholarship amount; the NCST is addressed by Article 338A.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly matches the constitutional commissions to their articles?
questions.explanation: Article 338 provides for the National Commission for Scheduled Castes and Article 338A for the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes. They are distinct constitutional commissions, not one combined present-day body.

questions.prompt: Which comparison correctly distinguishes the two protection statutes in today's notes?
options: The 1955 and 1989 titles are two names for the same Act
The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 addresses untouchability-related disabilities; the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 addresses specified atrocities against SC/ST members
The 1989 Act created the office of Governor
The 1955 Act is merely a non-binding study guideline
questions.explanation: The Acts are separate statutes with distinct titles, years and purposes. The 1955 Act is connected to the abolition of untouchability, while the 1989 Act addresses specified atrocities against SC/ST members and associated trial and relief arrangements. Detailed application requires the relevant provisions, not the titles alone.

review: Spend 5 minutes checking explanations, 5 minutes redoing errors without the notes, and 5 minutes writing a short recall sheet. Review correct guesses as well as wrong answers.

Score this set as correct minus wrong/3, with blanks scoring zero. For example, 11 correct, 3 wrong and 1 blank gives 10 net marks out of 15. This is learning feedback, not an official cut-off prediction.

Error-log fields: question ID; your answer; corrected answer; cause; one rule that prevents repetition. Useful labels today are appointing authority versus responsibility, wrong House, unmatched ratio base, unequal weights, changed observation count, wrong article and confused Act year.

Five-minute exit sheet: draw the Union–State executive comparison; solve one linked-ratio problem and one weighted mean; identify Articles 17, 46, 338 and 338A; and distinguish the 1955 and 1989 Acts in one sentence.
Reattempt wrong and guessed questions after 2, 7 and 21 days. Use part of those days' review slots so the total remains two hours. Keep repeat-attempt results separate from scores on fresh questions.
Start the next lesson with the two weakest distinctions from today. If you cannot explain why a distractor is wrong, keep the item in your review list even when you selected the correct option.

practice_method: First read the current syllabus and label every old question: current topic, changed topic, or outside the present syllabus. The current notification governs scope.

Hide answers before attempting. Some official archive files combine questions and keys; keep a working copy with the key concealed. AD archive files may omit distractor options, so use those as recall/problem exercises rather than valid timed MCQ mocks.

For papers with one mark per question and one-third negative marking, record raw practice score as correct minus wrong/3. Leave unanswered questions at zero. Apply deleted/revised-question treatment from the official final key when checking a historical paper.

Record paper/year/set, question number, syllabus topic, your answer, final-key answer, time, confidence, error type and next revision date. Separate concept gaps, calculation mistakes, misreading and unsupported guesses.
Reattempt wrong questions after 2 days, 7 days and 21 days without looking at the answer. Keep fresh-paper mock scores separate from reattempt scores.

For a 120-minute Group I paper, try roughly 70 minutes first pass, 40 revisits and 10 checking. For other posts, practise 75-minute half-papers plus 45-minute review within a two-hour day; these are sectional tests. A true 150-minute paper requires a separately available longer session. The official exam instructions take priority.

Use attempted-question accuracy, net score, time overruns and repeat-error rate to choose the next week's topics. A useful personal target is at least 75% accuracy on attempted questions with declining avoidable errors; it is not an official cut-off or selection prediction.

For descriptive mains practice, plan the answer, state the central argument, support it with relevant AP/Indian examples and finish within the prescribed time/word limit. Build writing practice gradually rather than waiting for the screening result.
